body:
FOUND 2026-08-11 by the T139 lane while fixing the server-side instance (PR #383). Same shape, different surface, not in T139's scope: `src/gateway/artifact-page.ts` around lines 156 and 178 bounds two distinct waits with a single budget — the pattern T139 proved is a SPEC-ACCURACY bug rather than a flake.

WHY IT MATTERS THE SAME WAY. A budget that covers both the thing being measured and the machinery that starts it does not measure the thing. On the server this made a legitimate render return a false 500 whenever the host was loaded past ~150 average — the failure blamed the bundle for the box. Whatever the browser-side equivalent is (a slow fetch, a slow parse, a contended tab), the same conflation means the page can report a budget overrun it did not observe. That is the H7 family: a report that can be false.

BEFORE BUILDING, MEASURE. T139's value came from reproducing the failure deliberately and recording the threshold, not from reasoning about the code. Do the same here: find the load or latency at which the shared budget misattributes, and record it in the ticket. If it turns out the two waits are genuinely bounded by the same promise on this surface, that is a valid answer — say so and close the ticket rather than splitting a timer for symmetry.

THE REPAIR, if measurement earns it: split the clocks, give the start-up wait its own ceiling and its own message (never a timeout message, which would claim the work ran), and put the ceiling in the operator's hands if it bounds anything an anonymous caller can occupy.

CARE, learned from T139's own review: a start-up ceiling that is generous widens the worst-case time one caller can hold a slot. If any slot on this surface is anonymous, that widening is a decision about availability, not a repair — state it in one line in the PR and hand the merge to Myk.

RAILS: two-sided at both levels — a slow start does not report a budget overrun, and a genuine overrun still does.

--- MEASURED 2026-08-12, and the measurement CHANGED the design.

INSTRUMENT. A real headless Chrome over CDP, running the SHIPPED `realmProgram()` bytes from a
loopback page, timing `new Worker(blob, {type:"module"})` to the realm's `live` message. Load came
from N busy-loop shells beside it. Box: 16 cores, WSL2. The harness was a throwaway; the numbers are
in the PR and in the shell's own comment.

SPAWN, the wait the shell charged to the render budget:

| load average | spawn p50 | spawn p90 | worst | over the 500 ms default |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ~0.3 (idle) | 4 ms | 7 ms | 9 ms | 0 of 40 |
| ~40 | 40 ms | 68 ms | 78 ms | 0 of 40 |
| ~150 | 91 ms | 108 ms | 113 ms | 0 of 40 |
| ~440 | 196 ms | 344 ms | 450 ms | 0 of 30 |
| ~550 | 291 ms | 579 ms | 803 ms | 4 of 30 |

A cold first spawn in a fresh tab is 10 ms at idle — not the worse case.

THE THRESHOLD, stated two ways. Against the 500 ms default, spawn starts crossing at load average
about 500 on a 16-core box, which is 31 times the core count. But the honest form is a RATIO: the
report is false whenever spawn exceeds `renderTimeoutMs`, and `renderTimeoutMs` is the operator's.
There is no clamp on it. At an operator-set 100 ms the misattribution begins at load about 150; at
50 ms, at load about 60. So the defect is not confined to an extreme box.

VERDICT: the defect is REAL and the fix is earned. Same shape as T139, different surface.

WHAT THE MEASUREMENT ALSO FOUND, which no reasoning had reached. The realm signals `live` when ITS
module has evaluated, which is BEFORE the bundle arrives. So the render window still carries the
bundle's own blob: import and module evaluation. Measured with a trivial bundle: 2 ms idle, 127 ms
median and 801 ms worst at load 550. It cannot be split further, because `import()` resolves only
after the bundle's top-level has run, so no signal can sit between the loader plumbing and the
bundle's own code. A trivial bundle can therefore still be reported as timing out past load about
500. The number is named in the shell comment and in the rail file's gap list; closing it would need
a wider operator budget, which is a §23.9 decision.

THE AVAILABILITY QUESTION, answered. No slot on this surface is anonymous. The clock runs in the
viewer's own tab and holds no store resource, so the ceiling is a page CONSTANT rather than an
operator option — unlike the server host's, where the ceiling bounds how long one anonymous caller
may hold a `maxPublicRenders` slot. The generous ceiling's real cost is a superseded worker
lingering, and the shell now tears those down at the moment they are superseded rather than at their
own clocks.

FOUND WHILE FIXING, and repaired here because each was inside the same twenty lines: the `live`
re-arm had no once-guard, so a bundle reaching a bare `postMessage` could hold the render clock open
forever; the mount-failure path returned before the epoch bump, so a render in flight could paint
over its refusal with a stale view; and the internal teardown shared the reporting ladder with
worker messages, so a bundle could post the shell's own `superseded` kind and silence its own fault.

FOUND AND NOT FIXED HERE: T160. A mediated read in flight survives a teardown, because the gesture
path has no epoch. That is the read path, not the clocks.
title: The browser-side renderer arms one number on two clocks — `artifact-page.ts` carries T139's defect shape
